turns.text: Hi, Rohan. Can you hear me clearly?
Hi, Elena. Yes, I can hear you. Is my audio okay?
It is. There was a brief delay when you joined, but it seems stable now. If it changes, we'll pause rather than talk over the connection.
Sounds good. Thank you.
We have about twenty-five minutes. I'll ask about your background, what you're looking for, and the practical remote setup. Then I'll explain the role and leave time for your questions.
Yes, that works for me.
Before we get into the main round, could you give me a brief description of yourself and what you've been working on recently?

I'm a platform engineer with seven and a half years of experience. At NimbusArc, an Indian cloud company, I work on the Kubernetes platform used by about eighty product teams. My current scope includes cluster upgrades, deployment guardrails, and the on-call mechanisms around them. Last year I led a move from team-owned ingress controllers to a managed gateway model. I wrote the migration design, built the admission checks with two engineers, and coordinated adoption with the highest-traffic teams. I don't manage people, but I mentor three engineers and lead cross-team technical work. I'm looking for a senior individual-contributor role with deeper reliability ownership on a distributed team.
Your resume says Lead Platform Engineer. Is that a people-management title?

No. At NimbusArc, 'Lead' is an individual-contributor title. I have no direct reports, compensation decisions, or performance reviews. I lead projects and the weekly platform design review, and I mentor engineers, but my manager owns the team. In a US leveling system I would expect calibration somewhere around senior engineer, depending on the breadth required. I would not map the word 'Lead' directly to staff or engineering manager.
Why move from a company where you already have broad platform scope?

The scale is meaningful, but most platform customers are internal teams in one country and major decisions still happen in a shared office window. The role here combines reliability engineering with an explicitly distributed operating model. I want to learn how a platform team supports autonomous teams across regions without relying on informal access. I'm also looking for more ownership of service-level objectives and capacity economics, not only cluster operations.
What specifically interested you in this role?

The posting describes a team responsible for deployment safety and workload isolation rather than a generic DevOps function. That matches my strongest experience. I also noticed that the first project is reducing noisy-neighbor incidents in a multi-tenant compute platform. I have handled similar symptoms, but your environment uses different primitives and a larger regional footprint. The problem is familiar enough that I can contribute and different enough that I will have to learn.
How hands-on are you today?

About sixty percent of my time is code, design, or operational debugging. The rest is review, planning, and mentoring. I write Go services and controllers, Terraform modules, and some policy code. I no longer take every ticket, but I still own implementation for risky parts of the projects I lead. I would not be happy in a role where 'senior' meant only meetings, and I also would not be effective if there were no time for design and leverage work.
Tell me about a project that did not land as planned.

For the gateway migration, I assumed teams would adopt a standard policy bundle if we provided automation. Two teams had legitimate custom routing behavior and delayed. My first response was to add more configuration, which made the interface worse for everyone. After a review, I separated an intentionally narrow common path from a documented exception process. Adoption was slower than my original quarter plan but operational incidents fell, and we stopped carrying unused flexibility. The miss was treating resistance as a tooling problem before understanding it.
What level are you targeting?

Senior individual contributor. I can lead a multi-team platform change and own an operational area, but I have less evidence setting direction across several independent platform domains. If your staff level requires organization-wide technical strategy, I would not claim that today. I would rather join at the level where expectations and evidence match than optimize the title.
What would a successful first year look like?

I would expect to become a trusted on-call owner, ship one meaningful reliability improvement, and make at least one operating mechanism better for teams in other time zones. Success would not be only learning the stack. It would include being able to explain why an incident class occurs, change the system or default that creates it, and leave the next engineer with clearer diagnosis and recovery paths.
Give me an example of reliability ownership rather than project delivery.

We had recurring node-pressure incidents that were mitigated by restarting workloads. I took a month of page data, separated application memory leaks from platform eviction behavior, and proposed safer requests and limits plus a diagnostic dashboard. I did not own every application fix, but I changed the admission defaults and the escalation evidence. Page volume fell, and teams could see whether the platform or workload needed action. The important difference was reducing the incident class, not closing one ticket quickly.
How do you decide when platform consistency is worth slowing a product team?

I first name the shared failure or cost the standard prevents. If the risk is security, tenant isolation, or an operational burden transferred to everyone, a guarded default is justified. If the difference is local style, I prefer a paved path and evidence rather than a mandate. I also provide an exception owner and expiry. A standard without a usable migration path turns platform authority into delay, while unlimited exceptions make the default meaningless.
Your current company is office-first. What evidence do you have for remote work?

My direct team is office-first, so this would be a change. However, the gateway project involved teams in Dublin and Singapore for almost a year. I ran design review asynchronously, kept decisions in an RFC, and used our overlap for unresolved risks. I know that is not identical to a remote-first company. The evidence I can offer is that I changed the work so teams did not need access to me in Hyderabad to make progress.
How did you keep that RFC from becoming a long document nobody read?

The main document stayed under six pages: decision, constraints, proposed interface, rejected options, migration, and open questions. Detailed benchmarks and policy examples lived in linked appendices. Every open question had an owner and closing date. I posted a two-paragraph change summary after each revision instead of asking everyone to reread it. That structure came after my first RFC reached eighteen pages and received very little useful review.
Describe a cross-time-zone misunderstanding.

I wrote that a gateway policy would be 'backward compatible,' meaning existing manifests would still deploy. The Dublin team interpreted it to mean request behavior would be identical. A header normalization changed for one route. We caught it before production, but the phrase hid two different contracts. I changed the RFC to separate configuration compatibility from runtime behavior and added traffic replay evidence. It was a precise language failure, not a time-zone failure, but limited overlap made the ambiguity cost a full day.
The team has an on-call rotation. What boundaries do you need?

I am comfortable with a defined rotation, including severe incidents outside the overlap window. I need the frequency, compensation or time-off policy, escalation path, and page volume to be transparent. I would be concerned if routine alerts regularly woke India-based engineers because the schedule was designed only around US hours. I want to share operational ownership, not avoid it, and I expect the system and rotation to improve when pages are noisy.
How do you mentor remotely?

I use small written design prompts and review the reasoning, not only the final code. For a newer engineer, I agree on when they should proceed independently and when risk requires a check-in. I also keep one predictable office hour so questions do not wait for a formal meeting. What I still have to learn is how to build rapport without shared office context; I would ask the team what has worked rather than assume the same habits transfer.
What would you do if a US teammate regularly schedules outside the agreed overlap?

I would first check whether the pattern reflects an incident, a calendar misunderstanding, or an actual expectation. Then I would state the agreed window and the effect directly, offer times inside it, and ask the manager to clarify the team norm if it continued. I would not silently attend and build resentment, and I would not treat one accidental meeting as disrespect.
Tell me about an incident handoff that crossed regions.

A certificate rollout began failing near the end of our India day. I wrote the affected cluster cohorts, current error rate, last safe version, rollback command, and the condition under which Dublin should continue versus stop. I stayed through the first rollback to verify the procedure, then handed over rather than remaining awake as a second commander. Dublin found one cohort I had missed and added it to the record. The next India shift could reconstruct both the action and the new evidence without a verbal retelling.
What was weak about that handoff?

I initially included several raw dashboards but did not state which graph was authoritative. Dublin asked before acting, which cost about fifteen minutes. After the incident I changed the template to name the decision metric, its query, and the expected delay. More links did not mean more clarity; the receiver needed one trusted measure and a clear fallback if it disagreed with logs.
This is employment through an EOR in India. Any concern?

No concern with the model itself. I would review which entity employs me, benefits, leave, intellectual-property language, termination terms, and how on-call expectations appear in the agreement. I understand the US company would direct the work while the EOR handles local employment. I would not expect US work authorization or a US payroll relationship.
The regular overlap is 7:30 to 11:00 a.m. Pacific. Does that work from Hyderabad?

It would place the overlap in my evening. Three and a half hours is workable if the rest of the schedule is flexible and we protect the window for collaboration rather than status. I would want the rotation and planning calendar early so my family can plan around later days. I could not sustain a full India daytime schedule plus four US hours.
Your notice period?

Ninety days contractually. My company has approved sixty-day releases for senior individual contributors after a documented handover, but I cannot guarantee that. I would plan for ninety in the process and explore a responsible reduction after a signed offer.
The team hopes for someone within eight weeks.

Then timing is a genuine risk. If eight weeks is a hard maximum, I don't want to hide the mismatch. If the company can carry a range and decide after the interviews, I am willing to proceed and prepare a detailed handover plan. I would not resign before an accepted written offer.
What compensation range are you considering?
Could you share the approved fixed-salary band and whether the equity is options or restricted shares? At this level, on-call, benefits, and the EOR structure affect how I compare the package.
Fixed salary is sixty-two to seventy-five lakh, plus options and local benefits.

That range is aligned. I would target the middle to upper portion if the scope matches the senior description, but I would evaluate the option terms, benefits, on-call load, and level after the technical loop. I don't need to anchor outside the stated band to continue. I would also want to understand the option exercise window and whether an EOR termination changes vesting, because headline grant size alone is not enough to compare equity.
Do you have any planned leave in the next four months?
I have one week of family travel booked in October. The dates are fixed, and I would disclose them before agreeing on a start date. Other than that, no planned absence.
I have what I need. What questions do you have for me?
How do you distinguish senior from staff on this platform team?

Senior engineers own services and multi-team projects. Staff engineers set direction across several platform areas and are accountable for technical alignment beyond one team. The current opening is senior, though we calibrate in the loop.
That matches how I described my evidence.
What is the actual on-call page volume, not only the rotation frequency?
The rotation is one week in seven. Median is two actionable pages per week, but one legacy scheduler creates bursts. Reducing that noise is an active goal.
The burst source is useful context. I would want to understand that early.
What decision mechanism has worked best across regions?
Short RFCs with a named decider and a deadline. The harder part is making dissent visible before the deadline; quiet does not always mean agreement.
I have seen the same issue and like the named-decider model.
Those were my main questions. Thank you for the context and for your time.

The next step is a platform debugging interview, then system design and a hiring-manager round. I need to review this screen with the manager. The recruiter team will contact you within four business days, and we will be explicit about whether the notice-period range still works.
Understood. Thank you, Elena. Have a good day.
You too, Rohan. Take care.
